generalizedRange: A secret canyon in Wollemi National Park, Australia
hook: Known only from fossils — until a ranger walked into its canyon.

story.text: In 1994, an off-duty parks ranger dropped into a remote canyon northwest of Sydney and stood among trees no living botanist had ever seen.
They were Wollemi pines — a conifer known only from fossils, its last trace about two million years old, its family a companion of the dinosaurs.
Botanists called the discovery the equivalent of finding a small dinosaur alive.
The tree is strange in person: dark bark that bubbles like chocolate, fern-like sprays of leaves, and trunks that multiply — some trees carry more than twenty.
Self-coppicing lets a single tree persist for centuries, trunk after trunk.
Only 46 adult trees and 43 juveniles remain in the wild, and their canyon is a state secret.
The secrecy is protection: one visitor's boots could carry in the root-rot pathogen that kills them.
In the Black Summer of 2019–20, firefighters and air tankers saved the only known grove as fire closed around it.
The insurance policy is planetary: cultivated Wollemi pines now grow in gardens across the world, and new translocated groves are taking root at secret sites inside the park.
To witness the Wollemi pine is to look after deep time itself — a living fossil that survived everything except, perhaps, us.

editorial.notes: Card v2 drafted from verified NSW Government and Botanic Gardens of Sydney pages — the catalog's first plant. Schema adapted honestly: 'diet' describes how a conifer feeds; the wild site is secret, so the region circle deliberately covers the whole national park. 'Coco Pops' bark folklore replaced by the sourced 'bubbling chocolate' wording; the fire is named only as the 2019-20 Black Summer per sources. The NSW-environment news page cited in research 404s to direct fetch, so it and its '835 saplings' figure were dropped; translocation is cited to NPWS instead.

stats.size: Up to 43 m — a forest giant

reproduction.text: Each tree carries both cone sexes — elongated pollen cones and spherical seed cones that ripen over eighteen months. And when seed fails, the tree endures anyway, sprouting new trunks from its own base.

insight.text: In 2021 the grove became New South Wales's first 'Asset of Intergenerational Significance' — the strongest legal protection the state can give.
